name: Big Five (OCEAN) Test
tagline: A detailed look at your personality across ten trait aspects.
intro: The Big Five, or OCEAN, model is the most widely researched framework in personality psychology. This detailed version splits each of the five traits into two aspects, giving you a profile on ten facets of who you are. Rate 100 short statements; it takes about five minutes.
seoDescription: Go beyond the basic five traits. This free 5-minute OCEAN test scores you on ten personality aspects and explains what each one means for your daily life.

intellect.name: Intellect
intellect.short: Part of Openness: your appetite for ideas, reasoning and intellectual challenge.
intellect.low: You prefer practical knowledge over theory and would rather act than analyse. Puzzles and debates for their own sake do not appeal to you much, and you trust experience more than abstract arguments. This keeps you focused on what is useful. Tip: when a complex decision comes up, give yourself a short, structured thinking moment, such as listing pros and cons, before acting. Learning one new topic in small doses can also keep your mind flexible.
intellect.mid: You enjoy thinking things through when the topic interests you, but you do not need constant intellectual stimulation. You can follow a complex argument and also appreciate a simple, practical answer. Tip: choose one area you are curious about and go deeper than usual, for example with a course or a challenging book. Notice whether you avoid hard problems out of habit or simply out of preference.
intellect.high: You love ideas, puzzles and complex questions. You learn quickly, enjoy debating and like to understand how and why things work. This makes you a strong problem solver. The pitfall is overthinking: you may analyse when action is needed or lose patience with people who think differently. Tip: set a time limit for analysis and then decide. When explaining ideas, check whether your listener is following before you go deeper.

aesthetics.name: Aesthetics
aesthetics.short: Part of Openness: your sensitivity to beauty, art, nature and inner experience.
aesthetics.low: You take a practical view of the world and are not strongly moved by art, poetry or design. You judge things by whether they work rather than how they look or feel. This keeps you level-headed and efficient. Tip: try to notice one beautiful detail each day, like light, a melody or a well-made object. Shared cultural outings can also be a good way to connect with people who value these experiences.
aesthetics.mid: You appreciate beauty and creativity in some forms, perhaps music or nature, without being swept away by them. You can enjoy a museum or a film, but you do not need art every day. Tip: discover which kinds of beauty affect you most and make a little room for them in your routine, such as a playlist for focused work or a weekly walk somewhere green.
aesthetics.high: You are deeply sensitive to beauty, art and atmosphere. Music, landscapes, stories and design can move you strongly, and you often notice details others pass by. This gives your life richness and fuels creativity. The pitfall is that harsh or ugly surroundings may drain you more than others. Tip: shape your environment so it inspires you, and give your creative side a regular outlet, such as drawing, writing or playing music.

industriousness.name: Industriousness
industriousness.short: Part of Conscientiousness: your drive, persistence and self-discipline.
industriousness.low: You work best when a task really interests you, and you find it hard to push through boring or long-term work. You may put things off or lose momentum halfway. This is not laziness; motivation simply depends strongly on interest for you. Tip: break big goals into very small steps with clear deadlines. Use external structure, like a work buddy or a timer, to get started, and reward yourself when you finish.
industriousness.mid: You can be driven and persistent when a goal matters to you, though your energy may dip on tasks you find dull. You usually get things done, sometimes with a last-minute push. Tip: identify the time of day when you focus best and protect it for your most important task. Tracking progress visibly, for example with a checklist, helps keep momentum on longer projects.
industriousness.high: You are hard-working, focused and persistent. You set goals, start right away and keep going until the job is done, even when it gets tedious. People see you as competent and dependable. The pitfall is overwork: you may struggle to switch off or feel guilty when resting. Tip: plan breaks and free time as firmly as your tasks. Ask yourself regularly whether your effort is aimed at the goals that matter most to you.

orderliness.name: Orderliness
orderliness.short: Part of Conscientiousness: your need for structure, neatness and routine.
orderliness.low: You are comfortable with a bit of chaos and do not mind if things are not perfectly arranged. You prefer flexibility to fixed routines and can improvise easily. This makes you adaptable. The pitfall is that you may lose time searching for things or forget details. Tip: create just a few simple systems for the essentials, such as one place for keys and documents and a single digital calendar. Small structure frees your mind.
orderliness.mid: You like a reasonable level of order without needing everything perfect. You keep important things organised and let less important things slide. You can follow a routine but also handle change. Tip: notice which areas cause you stress when they get messy, and give those a simple, fixed system. Everywhere else, allow yourself to stay relaxed and spend your energy on things that matter more to you.
orderliness.high: You love order, structure and routine. You keep things tidy, follow procedures and like to know exactly what will happen. This makes you precise and reliable. The pitfall is rigidity: unexpected changes or other people's mess can frustrate you, and perfectionism may slow you down. Tip: practise tolerating small imperfections on purpose. Agree on shared standards with others instead of assuming everyone sees order the way you do.

enthusiasm.name: Enthusiasm
enthusiasm.short: Part of Extraversion: your sociability, warmth and capacity for joy and excitement.
enthusiasm.low: You are reserved and calm in how you show positive feelings. You may enjoy company but do not seek it out often, and you tend to keep your excitement to yourself. Others may experience you as serious or hard to read. Tip: when you are pleased, say so out loud; people appreciate knowing. Plan small social moments with people you trust, so connection stays part of your life without draining you.
enthusiasm.mid: You enjoy people and fun, but you also value quiet moments. You can be lively and warm in good company and more reserved around strangers. This balance lets you connect without burning out. Tip: notice which activities and people genuinely lift your mood and make sure they appear regularly in your week. Saying yes to an occasional spontaneous invitation can bring unexpected joy.
enthusiasm.high: You are warm, outgoing and quick to feel joy and excitement. You make friends easily, show your feelings openly and bring energy into a room. People are often drawn to your cheerfulness. The pitfall is that you may chase stimulation and feel restless when life is quiet. Tip: balance exciting plans with calm recovery time. Check in with quieter friends too; your warmth can make them feel welcome if you leave space for them.

assertiveness.name: Assertiveness
assertiveness.short: Part of Extraversion: how readily you take charge, speak up and influence others.
assertiveness.low: You prefer to let others lead and rarely push your own views forward. You are a good listener and can support a team without needing the spotlight. The pitfall is that your ideas and needs may go unheard. Tip: prepare one point you want to make before each meeting and say it early. Practise expressing a preference, even about small things like where to eat; it builds confidence step by step.
assertiveness.mid: You can take the lead when the situation calls for it, but you are also happy to follow someone else. You speak up on topics you care about and stay quiet on others. Tip: pay attention to moments when you hold back although you have something valuable to say. In those moments, try stating your opinion clearly and briefly, then invite responses.
assertiveness.high: You are confident, decisive and comfortable taking charge. You speak your mind, influence others easily and do not shy away from leadership. Teams often look to you for direction. The pitfall is that you may dominate conversations or push decisions before others are ready. Tip: in discussions, ask others for their view before giving yours. Delegating real responsibility shows trust and helps you lead more effectively.

compassion.name: Compassion
compassion.short: Part of Agreeableness: your empathy, care and emotional concern for others.
compassion.low: You approach people's problems with a cool, rational eye. You are less swayed by emotions and can stay objective where others get caught up. This helps in tough decisions. The pitfall is that people may feel you do not care, even when you do. Tip: when someone shares a problem, first reflect back what they feel, for example 'that sounds frustrating', before offering advice. Small gestures of interest go a long way.
compassion.mid: You care about others and can be supportive, while also keeping some emotional distance. You help when you see a real need, but you do not take on everyone's problems. Tip: notice the people around you who might be struggling quietly and check in with them. At the same time, keep protecting your own energy; caring well also means knowing your limits.
compassion.high: You are deeply empathic and caring. You easily sense how others feel, are moved by their troubles and want to help. People trust you with their worries. The pitfall is compassion fatigue: you may absorb others' pain, neglect your own needs or struggle to set limits. Tip: remind yourself that listening is often enough; you do not have to fix everything. Plan time to recharge after emotionally heavy contact.

politeness.name: Politeness
politeness.short: Part of Agreeableness: your courtesy, modesty and respect for others and rules.
politeness.low: You are frank, independent and willing to challenge authority. You do not mind conflict and will push back when you disagree, even with people in charge. This makes you honest and hard to manipulate. The pitfall is that others may see you as confrontational or disrespectful. Tip: choose your battles; save open challenges for the issues that matter most. Phrasing criticism as a question can keep the conversation constructive.
politeness.mid: You are generally respectful and cooperative, but you will stand your ground when something feels unfair. You follow most norms while keeping your own judgement. Tip: notice whether you hold back disagreement out of politeness when it matters, or push back when it does not. Adjusting that balance helps you stay both respected and authentic, and it makes your agreement more meaningful when you do give it.
politeness.high: You are courteous, modest and respectful. You avoid offending others, follow social rules and rarely push yourself forward. People find you pleasant and easy to work with. The pitfall is that you may suppress disagreement, accept unfair treatment or undersell yourself. Tip: practise stating a different opinion calmly and politely; respect and honesty can go together. Make sure your contributions are visible, not just your good manners.

volatility.name: Volatility
volatility.short: Part of Neuroticism: how quickly you get upset, irritated or emotionally stirred.
volatility.low: You are even-tempered and slow to anger. Frustrations rarely get the better of you, and you keep your cool in heated moments. Others find you a steady presence. The pitfall is that you may hide irritation until it builds up or seem unaffected when emotions run high. Tip: express mild frustration early and calmly, so it does not pile up. Acknowledge others' emotions even when you feel calm yourself.
volatility.mid: You usually keep your emotions in check, but stress or provocation can sometimes get to you. You might snap now and then, then calm down fairly quickly. Tip: learn your personal warning signs, such as a tight jaw or racing thoughts, and take a short pause before reacting. Enough sleep and regular breaks make a noticeable difference to your patience.
volatility.high: Your emotions can rise quickly and strongly. You may get irritated, upset or agitated easily, and your mood can shift from moment to moment. This intensity also brings passion and honesty. The pitfall is reacting in ways you regret later. Tip: use a simple pause rule, such as counting to ten or leaving the room briefly, before responding. Physical activity helps release tension. If strong emotions disrupt your life, consider support from a qualified professional.

withdrawal.name: Withdrawal
withdrawal.short: Part of Neuroticism: your tendency towards worry, insecurity and low mood.
withdrawal.low: You are self-assured and rarely troubled by worry or self-doubt. You face challenges with confidence and do not dwell on failures. This resilience helps you take risks and recover from setbacks. The pitfall is that you might overlook real dangers or seem unaware of others' anxieties. Tip: before big decisions, ask a more cautious colleague what could go wrong. Show understanding when others feel insecure rather than urging them to just relax.
withdrawal.mid: You feel worry, doubt or sadness sometimes, especially under pressure, but they usually pass. You can see risks without being ruled by them. Tip: when worries start looping, write them down and note one thing you can actually do about each. Talking with someone you trust often shrinks concerns back to a realistic size and reminds you that you have handled difficult moments before.
withdrawal.high: You are prone to worry, self-doubt and low moods. You may feel easily discouraged, anxious about what others think or overwhelmed by setbacks. This sensitivity can make you careful and thoughtful, but it can also hold you back. Tip: challenge harsh self-talk by asking what you would say to a friend. Build small routines that steady you, such as exercise and regular sleep. If these feelings persist, consider talking to a qualified professional.

summary: Each Big Five trait is shown as two aspects, scored from 0 to 100 %: openness (intellect, aesthetics), conscientiousness (industriousness, orderliness), extraversion (enthusiasm, assertiveness), agreeableness (compassion, politeness) and neuroticism (volatility, withdrawal). No score is better than another. The results describe how you see yourself and are meant for self-reflection, not diagnosis.
